provision: Two successive replacement constitutions, one from the left, one from the right, both rejected by plebiscite

source.constitution: Draft of the Constitutional Convention (2022) and draft of the Constitutional Council (2023)

text_summary: The 2022 draft declared a plurinational, ecological, social state with rights of nature, gender parity and regional autonomy; the 2023 draft entrenched conservative positions on property, pensions, migration and the 'right to life of the unborn'.
period: Never in force; the 1980 constitution (amended 2005) remains
history: After the 2019 protests, 78.2% voted in October 2020 to write a new constitution. A Convention dominated by independents and the left delivered a 388-article text, one of the longest in the world; on 4 September 2022 it was rejected 61.8% to 38.2% with compulsory voting. Parliament then set up a 24-member Expert Commission (appointed in equal shares by left and right) whose draft reached near-unanimity, but the elected 50-seat Constitutional Council, where the Republican Party held 22 seats and the right a three-fifths majority, kept only 22.6% of the experts' articles intact. That 216-article text was rejected on 17 December 2023 by 55.7%. President Boric closed the process; Chile still lives under the Pinochet-era text.

assessment.reasoning: Both drafts were written by whichever side held a temporary supermajority and each read as a party programme rather than a framework; length, novelty and polarisation made both easy to campaign against. Undurraga (Expert Commission chair) argues the moderate expert draft would have passed if both blocs had defended it; others argue the electorate simply wanted order, not a new text.

lesson: A constitution that one bloc can write alone will be rejected by the other; keep the text short, framework-level and negotiated across the divide before it goes to the people.
